draft.title: Building a strong paragraph
card: A body paragraph argues one main point. Its first sentence, the topic sentence, states that point as a claim.
The next sentences support the claim with an example or evidence, such as an event, a detail or a quotation from the text.
Then you explain how the evidence proves the claim. This step is called analysis. Without it, the reader has only a list of facts.
A paragraph can end with a short sentence that links back to the claim. Keep to one main point so the paragraph stays focused.
draft.remember: Claim first, then evidence, then an explanation of how the evidence proves the claim.

a.q: Which sentence works best as the topic sentence of a body paragraph?
opts: The film shows that loyalty can be tested by danger
The film was released in the middle of last year
In one scene, two friends run down a long hallway
Many people go to the cinema on the weekend
a.why: A topic sentence states a claim that the rest of the paragraph can prove. The scene about the hallway is an example, so it belongs later as support. The sentence about the release date is a fact, not an argument.
a.clue: Which sentence makes a point that needs proving?

b.q: Priya writes a claim that the narrator feels lonely. She adds an example of the narrator eating lunch alone each day, then moves to a new point. What is missing from her paragraph?
opts: An explanation of how the example shows loneliness
A second claim about a different character
A topic sentence placed before the claim
A longer retelling of the whole story
b.why: Priya has a claim and an example, but she has not explained how eating alone proves the narrator is lonely. That analysis is the missing step. A second claim would break the focus on one main point.
b.clue: The example is there, but has she said what it proves?

a.best: The film shows that loyalty can be tested by danger

b.best: An explanation of how the example shows loneliness

problems.detail: The right option is the longest and the only one that repeats the stem's details ('example', 'loneliness'), so a student could pick it without knowing what analysis is. The clue ('has she said what it proves?') also nearly states the answer.
